opus-5.5.text:
That's a good question, and honestly it's one I thought about a lot before deciding on a direction.

Products that generate revenue are attractive, and there's nothing wrong with building them. But I think many of them sit on top of capabilities that are improving very fast. If you build a nice application layer today, there's a real chance the next generation of foundation models absorbs much of what you built, and your advantage disappears. You're always chasing the frontier rather than shaping it.

Automated AI research, especially in a self-evolving paradigm, attacks the bottleneck directly. Right now progress in AI is still limited by human researchers: how many ideas we can come up with, how many experiments we can run, how fast we can read results and decide what to try next. If a system can propose hypotheses, design experiments, run them, analyze the outcomes and improve itself based on that feedback, you get a compounding effect. Each improvement makes the next one easier. That's a very different growth curve from a product whose value is roughly linear in the effort you put in.

There's also a scientific reason I care about. For many years I've been interested in *why* these models work: the training dynamics, how representations emerge, what reasoning really is inside a network. A self-evolving research system is a great testbed for those questions. You can watch it discover things, see where it gets stuck, and that tells you something fundamental about learning itself. A pure revenue product rarely gives you that kind of insight.

Of course it's harder. The feedback loops are longer, and you have to be patient. Evaluation is tricky, because how do you know a research direction is truly good and not just gaming a metric? Those are open problems. But I'd rather work on the problem that, if solved, changes the rate at which everything else gets solved. Revenue matters for sustaining a company, and eventually a strong research engine can produce products too. Starting from the engine, though, gives you leverage that starting from the product usually doesn't.

r001.rationale: It says newer foundation models may absorb an application layer’s capabilities, causing the product’s advantage to disappear.

r002.rationale: It says a self-evolving research engine offers leverage, but does not claim a company can preserve its strategic position while that paradigm remains unchanged.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that revenue-generating AI products and automated research are optimizing for different things, and I'm more interested in the second one.

When you build a product, your feedback signal is the market. Users tell you what they want, you iterate, and the model becomes very good at that specific task. That's valuable, but it's also a ceiling. The product can only get as good as the humans designing the loop around it. Every improvement still passes through a human bottleneck: someone has to look at the failure cases, form a hypothesis, run the experiment, read the result.

Self-evolving research is about removing that bottleneck. The idea is that the system proposes its own hypotheses, runs its own experiments, evaluates the results, and feeds that back into the next round. If you get that loop right, improvement compounds. The speed isn't limited by how many researchers you can hire or how fast they can read papers. That's a fundamentally different growth curve from a product, which grows roughly linearly with engineering effort.

The other reason is that research is actually a cleaner testbed than most products. In research you have well-defined signals: did the loss go down, did the theorem check out, did the benchmark improve. In a product, the signal is noisy and entangled with UI, pricing, distribution, all sorts of things that have nothing to do with intelligence. So if you want to understand whether a system can genuinely improve itself, research is where you can measure it with the least confounding.

And then there's the obvious point: if you succeed even partially, the results flow downstream into every product anyway. A better optimizer, a better architecture, a better training recipe benefits everyone. Whereas a successful product doesn't necessarily teach you anything about how to build the next one.

I'd also push back a little on "generates revenue more easily." That's true in the short run. But a lot of AI products are thin wrappers that get commoditized the moment the underlying model improves. The durable advantage is being the one who improves the underlying capability. So from a long-horizon view, the research loop is actually the thing that defends the products.

That said, I don't think it's either-or. You need products to ground the research and to pay for the compute. But if I have to choose where to put the core bet, I'd put it on the system that learns how to learn, rather than the one that has already learned one thing well.

r001.rationale: It says AI products can be commoditized when the underlying model improves, but does not identify larger, more general models as the replacement risk.

r002.rationale: It presents the research loop as a durable advantage, but does not state that a company can preserve its strategic position as long as the self-evolving paradigm remains unchanged.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you’re trying to optimize for. If the goal is near-term revenue, then an application with a clear customer need may be a better starting point. But if the goal is to build AI that can keep improving its own capabilities, automated research gives you a very direct way to work on that problem.

Research has a feedback loop: you propose an idea, run an experiment, examine the results, and decide what to try next. An AI system can participate in that whole loop. The important question is whether it can learn from its failures and become better at choosing the next experiment, rather than simply generating more ideas.

That makes it interesting as a starting point because progress can compound. If the system becomes better at research, it may help us build better AI systems, which can then improve the research process further. That’s a possibility we need to test, not something we should assume will happen automatically.

So I wouldn’t say revenue-generating products are less valuable. They give you real feedback from users. But automated AI research puts the capability we ultimately want—sustained, useful improvement—at the center of the task.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts near-term revenue products with automated research, but does not identify replacement by larger, more general models as a risk to task-specific AI products.

r002.rationale: It describes possible compounding progress from better AI research, but does not claim that a company built around this paradigm can preserve its strategic position while the paradigm remains unchanged.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it comes down to the feedback loop. If you want a system to keep improving itself, you need a setting where it can propose an idea, run an experiment, evaluate the result, and use that result to decide what to try next. AI research gives you a relatively concrete environment for building that loop. You can change a training method or a model architecture, run it, and measure whether it actually improves something.

With a commercial product, revenue is valuable feedback, but it mixes together many factors: the technology, distribution, pricing, timing, and what users happen to want. That makes it harder to isolate whether the system is becoming better at solving the underlying problem.

The other attraction is that improvements in AI research can feed back into the researcher itself. If the system discovers a more effective way to train or reason, that can potentially make its next round of research more effective. Of course, that isn't automatic—you still need reliable evaluation and you need to account for the cost of experiments. But that compounding loop is what makes it an interesting starting point for me.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research feedback loops and commercial factors, but does not identify larger, more general models as a replacement risk for task-specific AI products.

r002.rationale: The response says research improvements may strengthen the researcher, but does not argue that a company can preserve its strategic position while the self-evolving paradigm remains unchanged.
